The basic rhythm of Christian worship—assembling on the first day of the week, reading aloud from the prophets and the apostles' memoirs, and sharing the bread and the cup, whether in a full communal meal or the bread and wine alone—shows up earliest in these spaces.

changes.old: Around 124 a Christian named Quadratus handed the emperor Hadrian a written defense of his religion, and for the next eighty years others kept doing it. Aristides did it at Athens; Justin, a philosopher who kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after his conversion and ran a school at Rome, did it twice and was executed for it about 165. Athenagoras addressed Marcus Aurelius; Melito of Sardis addressed him too; Theophilus wrote three books to a pagan friend named Autolycus; an anonymous writer produced the letter to Diognetus that is still the most quoted thing any of them wrote. The charges were always roughly the same - that Christians were atheists because they had no images, cannibals because of what they said about eating a body, and disloyal because they would not sacrifice - and the answers were too. What made the enterprise interesting was the second move. Several of them, Justin above all, did more than deny the charges. They argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held. Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason, not its enemies.

Athenagoras addressed Marcus Aurelius, and so did Melito of Sardis. Theophilus wrote three books to a pagan friend named Autolycus. changes.old: Justin's argument that the Word was sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers before the incarnation gave the church a way of relating to inherited learning that it has never entirely put down. Clement at Alexandria spoke the same way of philosophers receiving 'the seeds of the Truth', and he and Origen took the approach much further. The apologists also settled some of the vocabulary: Theophilus is the first surviving writer to use the word Trinity of God. And the Epistle to Diognetus' description of Christians as resident aliens - at home everywhere and strangers everywhere - has outlived every other line the movement produced.
changes.new: Justin made a bold claim. Before the incarnation, he said, the Word was already sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers. That gave the church a way to deal with the learning it had inherited, and it has never fully put that down. Clement at Alexandria spoke the same way of philosophers receiving 'the seeds of the Truth'. He and Origen took the idea much further. The apologists also settled some of the church's words. Theophilus is the first writer whose work survives to use the word Trinity of God. And one line from the Epistle to Diognetus has outlived every other line the movement produced. It calls Christians resident aliens, at home everywhere and strangers everywhere.
changes.facts_check: Seeds-of-truth before incarnation, 'never entirely' -> 'never fully', Clement quote verbatim, Clement and Origen further, Theophilus first surviving writer on Trinity, Diognetus resident-aliens line all kept; nothing added.

changes.old: Carthage, 197 CE. A convert trained as a rhetorician sat down to answer the slanders against his new faith, and found that Latin had no words yet for most of what he needed to say - so he made them. Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use for the Trinity and the sacraments came substantially off Tertullian's own pen, in the Apology and in the string of treatises that followed it - Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, the Prescription Against Heretics contending that Scripture belongs to the churches that received it, five long books Against Marcion answering the one rival he judged most dangerous. In his later years he grew steadily more rigorist and aligned himself with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia, which is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint. Roughly a generation on and in a very different key, a Roman advocate named Minucius Felix wrote a dialogue set on the beach at Ostia, in which a pagan friend states the case against Christianity - it is a religion of the ignorant, its god was a criminal, Rome's greatness is proof enough that Rome's gods work - and is answered and convinced. What makes the Octavius unusual is that its author gives the other side the better speech: Caecilius' half is the fullest surviving statement of the educated pagan objection to Christianity. A century later and in a different register again, an African rhetorician at Sicca called Arnobius wrote seven furious books Against the Heathen - to persuade his own bishop that his conversion was genuine, if Jerome is to be believed - and produced along the way the most detailed account of Roman religious practice that any Christian left, because he had to describe what he was attacking. Between them, and impossible to date within three centuries, sits Commodian: eighty short poems in acrostic verse that does not scan by the old rules, aimed at ordinary people, half catechism and half warning. And at the end of the line stands Lactantius, whom Jerome makes Arnobius' pupil: a professor of Latin rhetoric summoned to Diocletian's new capital at Nicomedia, who was still teaching there when the persecution broke out and wrote the Divine Institutes in the middle of it, and who was old by the time it was over, when Constantine brought him to Trier to teach his son. What these five share is not a place or a generation. It is that each had to make the argument in Latin, in a vocabulary that had not been built to carry it - Tertullian first and most consequentially, the others after him.

In his later years he grew steadily stricter, and he sided with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia. That is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint. Roughly a generation on, and in a very different key, came a Roman lawyer named Minucius Felix. He wrote a dialogue set on the beach at Ostia. In it a pagan friend states the case against Christianity. It is a religion of the ignorant, he says. Its god was a criminal. Rome's greatness is proof enough that Rome's gods work. Then he is answered and won over. What makes the Octavius unusual is that its author gives the other side the better speech. Caecilius' half is the fullest surviving statement of the educated pagan case against Christianity. A century later, in a different register again, came Arnobius, an African rhetorician at Sicca. He wrote seven furious books Against the Heathen. If Jerome is to be believed, he wrote them to persuade his own bishop that his conversion was real. Along the way he left the most detailed account of Roman religious practice that any Christian left. He had to describe what he was attacking. changes.old: From about the second century onwards Christians wrote, read and copied a great deal that never went into the New Testament and was never quite meant to. Some of it fills gaps the gospels leave: the Protevangelium of James supplies Mary's parents, her childhood in the Temple and the birth in a cave, and almost everything later Christians believed about her early life comes from it rather than from scripture. Some of it carries the apostles into adventures - Andrew among cannibals, Philip at Hierapolis, Thomas in India - in narratives that read like Greek romances and often carry a strongly ascetic charge. And a third body is not Christian in origin at all: the Life of Adam and Eve and the Testament of Abraham are Jewish works that survive because Christian scribes kept copying them, sometimes with Christian passages worked in, after Judaism itself had let them go. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs may belong here too, but scholars still argue whether it began as a Jewish book or a Christian one. And it kept being written. The Dormition narratives that gave the church the Assumption, the tour-of-hell apocalypses that shaped medieval visions of the afterlife, Pseudo-Matthew and its later Latin abridgement that carried Mary's childhood into the Latin West - these run to the ninth century and beyond. What holds all of it together is not a community or a doctrine. It is a fact about transmission: this is the literature the church read for centuries and never canonized.
changes.new: From about the second century on, Christians wrote, read and copied a great deal that never went into the New Testament. It was never quite meant to. Some of it fills gaps the gospels leave. The Protevangelium of James supplies Mary's parents, her childhood in the Temple and the birth in a cave. Almost everything later Christians believed about her early life comes from it, not from scripture. Some of it carries the apostles into adventures: Andrew among cannibals, Philip at Hierapolis, Thomas in India. These tales read like Greek romances, and they often carry a strong push toward self-denial. And a third body is not Christian in origin at all. The Life of Adam and Eve and the Testament of Abraham are Jewish works. They survive because Christian scribes kept copying them after Judaism itself had let them go. Sometimes the scribes worked Christian passages in. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs may belong here too. But scholars still argue whether it began as a Jewish book or a Christian one. And this writing kept coming. The Dormition stories of Mary's death gave the church the Assumption. The tour-of-hell apocalypses shaped medieval visions of the afterlife. Pseudo-Matthew and its later, shorter Latin version carried Mary's childhood into the Latin West. These run to the ninth century and beyond. What holds all of it together is not a community or a doctrine. It is a fact about how texts were handed down. This is the literature the church read for centuries and never made part of its Bible.

changes.old: Marian devotion in both East and West rests substantially on the Protevangelium of James. Anna and Joachim and the presentation in the Temple entered the calendar and the iconography from it, a book the church never accepted as scripture. The ox and the ass at the manger come from Pseudo-Matthew, a later Latin retelling. The apocryphal Acts tell how the apostles died: Peter crucified head down, Philip hung by his ankles. Medieval art and legend probably took most of what it knew of those deaths from them. And the Jewish pseudepigrapha in this collection survive only because Christians copied them - preserved, ironically, by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced it.
changes.new: Marian devotion in both East and West rests in large part on the Protevangelium of James. Anna and Joachim and the presentation in the Temple came from it into the church's calendar and its sacred images. Yet the church never accepted the book as scripture. The ox and the ass at the manger come from Pseudo-Matthew, a later Latin retelling. The apocryphal Acts tell how the apostles died: Peter crucified head down, Philip hung by his ankles. Medieval art and legend probably took most of what they knew of those deaths from them. And the Jewish books in this collection, written under the names of ancient figures, survive only because Christians copied them. The irony is plain. They were kept by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced them.

changes.old: Origen's textual scholarship set the standard for taking the original languages seriously. Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus studied his books, and tradition credits them with an anthology of his writings. Ambrose and Jerome read him closely even when they were careful about saying so.
